title: Class 6 Maths Coordinate Geometry: Plotting Points Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Coordinate Geometry Made Simple
meta_desc: Learn Class 6 maths coordinate geometry: x-axis, y-axis, origin, ordered pairs and plotting points, with a solved map case study and a free quiz.
excerpt: The x-axis, the y-axis, the origin, and those little brackets like (3, 4) — here is how the ICSE Class 6 coordinate geometry chapter actually fits together, with a solved map case study and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Class 6 student a grid and ask them to mark the point (3, 4), and nine times out of ten the first attempt goes up 3 and across 4 — the exact opposite of what the brackets mean. That one mix-up is the whole story of class 6 maths coordinate geometry: once a child truly gets that the first number is the horizontal step and the second is the vertical step, the rest of the ICSE chapter falls into place quickly. This chapter stays entirely in the first quadrant, so there are no negative numbers to worry about yet — just a clean grid, two axes, and pairs of counting numbers.

In my experience with sixth-graders, the trouble is almost never the maths. It is the vocabulary landing all at once: axis, origin, ordered pair, coordinate. So let us take them one at a time, the way the chapter itself does.

The two axes and the origin

Draw two number lines that cross at a right angle. The horizontal one is the x-axis. The vertical one is the y-axis. The single point where they meet — the corner from which everything is measured — is the origin, and it sits at (0, 0). Every point on the grid is described by how far right you walk along the x-axis and how far up you climb along the y-axis.

I tell students to picture the origin as the front gate of their house. To describe where the neighbour’s dog is buried, you say ‘three gates to the right, then four gates up’. You always start at the gate, always go across first, then up. That fixed order is the heart of the chapter.

Ordered pairs: why (3, 4) is not (4, 3)

An ordered pair is two numbers written inside brackets with a comma between them, like (3, 4). The word ordered is doing real work — the order is not optional. The first number is the x-coordinate (steps right), the second is the y-coordinate (steps up).

The comma rule that saves marks

So (3, 4) means walk 3 right and 4 up. But (4, 3) means walk 4 right and 3 up — a completely different spot on the grid. Swapping the numbers is the single most common mistake in the chapter, and it is worth drilling until it feels automatic. A quick chant helps: along the corridor, then up the stairs.

Plotting points and reading them back

Plotting is turning a pair of numbers into a dot. Reading is the reverse — you are handed a dot and asked for its coordinates. A student needs both directions, because ICSE questions freely switch between ‘plot P(2, 5)’ and ‘write the coordinates of the point marked Q’.

Here is a small table of points to plot in the first quadrant, and what each instruction actually asks you to do.

PointOrdered pairSteps right (x)Steps up (y)
A(2, 3)23
B(5, 1)51
C(0, 4)04
D(6, 0)60
E(4, 4)44

Notice C and D. Point C(0, 4) has zero steps right, so it sits on the y-axis. Point D(6, 0) has zero steps up, so it sits on the x-axis. This catches students out, and examiners know it — a coordinate of 0 means ‘do not move at all in that direction’, which is a genuinely useful thing to notice, because it tells you a point lives on an axis without even plotting it.

Joining points to make shapes

Once several points are plotted, joining them in order draws a shape — and this is where the chapter suddenly feels worth the effort. Plot P(2, 2), Q(6, 2), R(6, 5) and S(2, 5), then join P to Q to R to S and back to P, and a rectangle appears. Change one coordinate and the shape changes. This is the quiet bridge from arithmetic to geometry, and it is why the topic sits under ‘coordinate geometry’ at all.

  • Plot the points lightly first, then join with a ruler.
  • Join them in the order given — skipping around gives a tangled mess, not a shape.
  • Count squares carefully; being one square off moves the whole figure.
  • For a closed shape, remember to join the last point back to the first.

A worked case study: the school map grid

Real questions rarely say ‘plot (3, 4)’. They wrap it in a story, and that is exactly what the case-study format practises. Here is one.

Riya draws a grid map of her school. The main gate is the origin (0, 0). Each square on her map is 10 metres. On her grid, the library is at (3, 2), the canteen is at (3, 5), and the science lab is at (6, 5).

Question 1: How far east is the library from the gate?

The x-coordinate of the library is 3, so it is 3 squares east. Each square is 10 metres, so the library is 3 × 10 = 30 metres east of the gate.

Question 2: What is special about the library and the canteen?

Both have an x-coordinate of 3 — (3, 2) and (3, 5). They line up vertically, one directly above the other. Points that share an x-coordinate always sit on the same vertical line.

Question 3: How far apart are the canteen and the science lab?

The canteen is (3, 5) and the lab is (6, 5). Same y-coordinate, so they are on the same horizontal line. The gap in x is 6 − 3 = 3 squares, which is 3 × 10 = 30 metres. Reading distance straight off the coordinates — without a ruler — is the payoff of understanding the grid, and it is the exact skill the case studies are built to train.

quiz.title: Class 6 Coordinate Geometry Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the x-axis, y-axis, origin, ordered pairs and plotting points in the first quadrant. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 coordinate geometry in the first quadrant

questions.q: What are the coordinates of the origin?
questions.explanation: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis meet, and it is always (0, 0).

questions.q: In the ordered pair (3, 4), what does the 3 tell you?
options: Move 3 units right along the x-axis
questions.explanation: The first number is the x-coordinate: steps to the right along the x-axis. The 4 is then steps up.

questions.q: Which point lies on the x-axis?
questions.explanation: A point on the x-axis has a y-coordinate of 0, so (5, 0) sits on the x-axis.

questions.q: Is the point (2, 6) the same as (6, 2)?
options: Only if both are on an axis
questions.explanation: An ordered pair depends on order. (2, 6) is 2 right and 6 up; (6, 2) is 6 right and 2 up.

questions.q: A point is 4 units right and 0 units up. Where is it?
questions.explanation: Zero steps up means it stays on the x-axis, at (4, 0).

questions.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
questions.explanation: A point on the y-axis has an x-coordinate of 0, so (0, 7) sits on the y-axis.

questions.q: The points P(2, 3) and Q(2, 8) share the same x-coordinate. How do they line up?
questions.explanation: Points with the same x-coordinate line up vertically, one directly above the other.

questions.q: You plot A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(4, 4), D(1, 4) and join them in order. What shape do you get?
questions.explanation: The four points are equal steps apart, so joining them in order makes a square with side 3 units.

faq.q: Does Class 6 coordinate geometry use negative numbers?
faq.a: No. The ICSE Class 6 chapter stays in the first quadrant, so all coordinates are 0 or positive whole numbers. Negative coordinates and the full four-quadrant plane come in later classes.

faq.q: What is the difference between the x-axis and the y-axis?
faq.a: The x-axis is the horizontal number line; the y-axis is the vertical one. They cross at the origin (0, 0). The x-coordinate is measured along the x-axis, the y-coordinate along the y-axis.
Because the pair is ordered. In (3, 4) you go 3 right then 4 up; in (4, 3) you go 4 right then 3 up — two different points. Always read along the corridor first, then up the stairs.

faq.q: How do I help my child stop swapping the coordinates?
faq.a: Use one fixed phrase every time, such as ‘across, then up’, and always plot the x-step before the y-step. A few days of the same routine makes it automatic, and the swapping mistake disappears.
